title: Heat Sources and Heat Transfer
seo_title: Year 3 Science: Heat Sources and Heat Transfer Worksheets (Australian Curriculum)
standard_text: Identify sources of heat energy and describe how heat moves through and between objects, including conductors and insulators (summary of the Australian Curriculum v9.0 Science content description).
meta_desc: Free Year 3 science worksheets on heat: sources of heat, how heat moves from hot to cold, reading thermometers, and conductors and insulators such as metal, wood, wool and an esky. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Heat moves from hot to cold.
key_sub: Conductors let heat move quickly; insulators slow it down.
body_html:
How to think about it

Heat always moves from a hotter object to a colder one.

  • Heat sources give off heat: the Sun, fire, a barbecue, a heater, your body.
  • Metals are good conductors: heat moves through them quickly.
  • Wood, plastic, wool and air are insulators: they slow heat moving, keeping hot things hot and cold things cold.
Example

Ice block in your hand. Which way does heat move?

your hand is warmer

Answer: from your hand to the ice

Example

Best handle for a frying pan?

the handle must not get hot

Answer: wood or plastic (an insulator)

Common mistakes

  • Thinking 'cold' flows into things (heat flows out of them).
  • Thinking a jumper makes its own heat.
  • Thinking metal is colder than wood in the same room (it only feels colder because it conducts heat away).

faq.a: Heat moves from a hotter object or place to a colder one until they are the same temperature.

faq.q: What is the difference between a conductor and an insulator of heat?
faq.a: A conductor, such as metal, lets heat move through it quickly. An insulator, such as wood, plastic or wool, slows heat down.

faq.q: Why does metal feel colder than wood in the same room?
faq.a: Both are at the same temperature, but metal conducts heat away from your hand faster, so it feels colder.

from a hotter object to a colder object

items.q: When you hold an ice block, what happens to the heat in your hand?
c: Cold moves from the ice into your hand.
Heat moves from your hand into the ice block.
Heat moves from the ice to your hand.
items.e: That is why your hand feels cold.

items.q: Which way does heat always move?
c: from a colder object to a hotter object
from a hotter object to a colder object
items.e: Cold does not flow; heat moves out of hot things.

items.q: What does a solar hot water system use to heat water?
items.e: Many Australian roofs have solar panels or solar hot water.

items.q: Which of these is a source of heat?

items.e: A heat source gives off heat: the Sun, fire, electric heaters and even your body.

items.e: A block of wood at room temperature does not give off heat.

items.q: Which of these is a source of heat?

items.q: Why do saucepans often have plastic or wooden handles?
c: Plastic and wood are poor conductors, so the handle stays cool.
items.e: Insulators protect your hand.

items.q: Why does beach sand feel hotter than the water on a sunny day?
c: Sand heats up faster than water in the sun.
The water is far from the Sun.
items.e: Different materials heat up at different rates.

items.q: What is the unit of temperature we use in science?
items.e: Water freezes at 0 °C and boils at 100 °C.

items.q: When does heat stop flowing between two objects?
c: when they are at the same temperature
when the hotter one is empty
items.e: There is no more heat flow when the temperatures are equal.

items.q: What is the main source of heat for Earth?
items.e: Sunlight warms the land, sea and air.

items.q: Why does a cold drink become warm when left on a table?
c: It loses cold to the air.
It gains heat from the warmer air around it.
items.e: Heat flows from the warmer air into the drink.

items.q: Hot soup touches a metal spoon. In which direction does heat flow?
c: from a metal spoon to hot soup
from hot soup to a metal spoon
items.e: Heat flows from a hotter object to a colder one.

items.q: A cold towel touches the forehead of a person with a fever. Which one loses heat?
c: the forehead of a person with a fever
items.e: The hotter object loses heat to the colder one.

items.q: Hot water at 60 °C is mixed with cold water at 10 °C. What could the temperature of the mixture be?
items.e: The mixture is between the two temperatures: the hot water loses heat and the cold water gains heat.

items.q: Water is heated from 25 °C to 60 °C. What happened to it?
c: It gained heat and its temperature rose.
items.e: Gaining heat raises the temperature.

items.q: A sunny road touches your bare feet. Which one loses heat?
items.e: The hotter object loses heat to the colder one.

items.q: Which tool measures how hot something is?
items.e: Temperature is measured in degrees Celsius (°C).

items.q: Hot water at 70 °C is mixed with cold water at 20 °C. What could the temperature of the mixture be?
items.e: The mixture is between the two temperatures: the hot water loses heat and the cold water gains heat.

items.q: Hot water at 80 °C is mixed with cold water at 30 °C. What could the temperature of the mixture be?
items.e: The mixture is between the two temperatures: the hot water loses heat and the cold water gains heat.

items.q: What happens to most things when they lose heat?
items.e: Contract means get smaller.

items.q: How does an esky keep drinks cold?
c: Its walls are insulators that slow heat moving in from outside.
items.e: Insulators slow heat movement.

items.q: Hot soup touches a metal spoon. Which one gains heat?
items.e: The colder object gains heat from the hotter one.

items.q: A cold can of drink touches the air in the room. In which direction does heat flow?
c: from a cold can of drink to the air in the room
from the air in the room to a cold can of drink
items.e: Heat flows from a hotter object to a colder one.

items.q: A cold towel touches the forehead of a person with a fever. Which one gains heat?
c: the forehead of a person with a fever
items.e: The colder object gains heat from the hotter one.

items.q: Why do we feel cold when we hold an ice cube?
c: Cold moves from the ice into our hand.
Our hand loses heat to the ice.
Ice is a source of heat.
items.e: Heat flows from our warm hand to the colder ice.

items.q: A cup of water at 90 °C is left in a room at 28 °C for a long time. What will its final temperature be?
items.e: It loses heat until it reaches the temperature of the surroundings.

items.q: Hot soup touches a metal spoon. Which one loses heat?
items.e: The hotter object loses heat to the colder one.

items.q: Why does a metal slide feel very hot on a summer afternoon?
c: The slide is near a heater.
The Sun heats the metal and metal passes heat quickly into your skin.
items.e: Metal is a good conductor of heat.

items.q: A cup of hot tea touches the air in the room. In which direction does heat flow?
c: from a cup of hot tea to the air in the room
from the air in the room to a cup of hot tea
items.e: Heat flows from a hotter object to a colder one.

items.q: Why do some flasks have a space with very little air between two walls?
c: Heat cannot flow easily across the space.
The space lets heat in faster.
The space makes the flask heavier.
items.e: This keeps hot drinks hot and cold drinks cold.

items.q: Why is a paper cup with a cardboard sleeve used for a cup for hot coffee to take away?
c: It is the most colourful material.
The sleeve is a poor conductor of heat, so it protects your hand.
It is a good conductor of heat, so heat flows through it quickly.
items.e: Choose a material by how well it conducts heat.

items.q: Why are the handles of kettles often made of plastic?
c: Plastic is a poor conductor of heat.
Plastic is a good conductor of heat.
items.e: The handle stays cool enough to hold.

items.q: Why do pots have plastic or wooden handles?
c: These materials are poor conductors of heat, so the handles stay cool.
items.e: Heat flows slowly through plastic and wood.

items.q: Which statement is correct?
c: Poor conductors only keep things hot.
Poor conductors of heat can keep things hot and keep things cold.
Good conductors keep things cold for longer.
items.e: They slow down heat flow in either direction.

items.q: What is a good conductor of heat?
c: a material that gives out heat
a material that is always cold
a material that lets heat flow through it quickly
a material that stops all heat
items.e: Metals are good conductors of heat.

items.q: Why is polystyrene used for an esky for drinks?
c: It is a good conductor of heat, so heat flows through it quickly.
It is a poor conductor of heat, so heat from outside enters slowly and the drinks stay cold.
It is the most colourful material.
items.e: Choose a material by how well it conducts heat.

items.q: Which group of materials are good conductors of heat?
items.e: Copper, aluminium and steel conduct heat well.

items.q: Which material is best for the handle of a frying pan?
items.e: It is a poor conductor of heat, so the handle does not get too hot to hold.

items.q: A metal railing and a wooden bench are both in the sun at noon. Why does the railing feel hotter?
c: The railing is always hotter than wood.
Metal conducts heat into your hand faster.
The bench is in the shade.
items.e: Good conductors move heat quickly.

items.q: What is a poor conductor of heat?
c: a material that lets heat flow through it slowly
a material that is always warm
a material that lets heat flow quickly
items.e: Wood, plastic and polystyrene are poor conductors.

items.q: Which would keep a drink cold for the longest?
items.e: Plastic and trapped air are poor conductors.

items.q: Why do we wear thick clothes in a cold country?
c: The clothes are poor conductors of heat and slow down heat loss from the body.
items.e: Clothes do not make heat.

items.q: Why does a person feel cold standing barefoot on a tiled floor but not on a carpet?
c: Tiles conduct heat away from the feet faster than the carpet does.
Tiles are colder than carpet in the same room.
items.e: Carpet is a poorer conductor.

items.q: Which material is best for a baking tray?
items.e: It is a good conductor of heat, so the food cooks evenly.

items.q: A metal spoon and a wooden spoon have been in the same room all day. Why does the metal spoon feel colder?
c: The metal spoon is at a lower temperature.
Metal conducts heat away from your hand faster.
items.e: Both are at room temperature.

items.q: Why does a polystyrene box keep fish cold at the market?
c: Polystyrene is a poor conductor of heat, so heat from the air enters slowly.
items.e: Poor conductors slow down heat gain as well as heat loss.

items.q: Why is aluminium used for a baking tray?
c: It is the most colourful material.
It is a poor conductor of heat, so heat flows through it slowly.
It is a good conductor of heat, so the food cooks evenly.
items.e: Choose a material by how well it conducts heat.

items.q: Why do birds fluff up their feathers on a cold morning?
c: to trap more air, a poor conductor of heat
items.e: Trapped air slows down heat loss.

items.q: Why is rubber used for the soles of shoes for walking on a hot road?
c: It is a good conductor of heat, so heat flows through it quickly.
It is a poor conductor of heat, so the feet do not get burnt.
It is the most colourful material.
items.e: Choose a material by how well it conducts heat.

items.e: More water at the same starting temperature has more heat to lose.
